title: C# Questions & Answers - Public & Private Access Modifier
sourceFile: Public & Private Access Modifier - C# Questions & Answers - Sanfoundry.html
description: This section of our 1000+ C# multiple choice questions focuses on public and private access modifiers in C# Programming Language.

questions.question: Which of these is used as a default specifier for a member of a class if no access specifier is explicitly used?
questions.explanation: In C#, if no access modifier is specified for a class member (field, property, or method), it defaults to 'private'.

questions.question: Which of these is used to access members of a class before an object of that class is created?
questions.explanation: Static members belong to the class itself rather than any specific instance. They can be accessed using the class name without creating an object.

questions.question: Which of these base class member types are accessible to members of a derived class?
questions.explanation: The 'protected' keyword ensures that a member is accessible within its own class and by derived class instances.

questions.question: What is the process by which we can control parts of a program that can access the members of a class?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is one of the pillars of OOP that binds together code and data, and keeps both safe from outside interference and misuse via access modifiers.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation: For obj1: add(2, 3) -> x = 2+3=5, y = 5+3=8. For obj2: add(5, 2) -> x = 5+2=7, y = 7+2=9. Printing obj1.x (5) and obj2.y (9) results in '5 9'.

questions.question: Which of these are valid accessibility modifiers in C#?

options.text: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, private protected

questions.explanation: C# supports 6 access levels: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, and private protected (available in later versions).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: A base class member function can access public members of a derived class
An object of a derived class cannot access private members of the base class
Private members of a base class are not accessible by derived class member functions

questions.explanation: Inheritance is one-way. A base class has no knowledge of the members defined in its derived classes, even if those members are public.

questions.question: Which of these access specifiers must be used for the Main() method in C#?
questions.explanation: In C#, the Main method (entry point) does not require a specific access modifier. It can be public, internal, or even private, and the runtime will still be able to execute it.
